v.trust.p1: Barnard's Star is so bright that the centre of its image is saturated: in this exposure {sat} pixels hit the detector's limit. They are flat white and carry no position information. A naive method that looks at the bright centre measures the shape of that white blob, not the star. Our fit uses the {fit} unsaturated pixels around it.
v.trust.p2: We fit the star's shape to the unsaturated wings around the core instead, and tie every exposure to Gaia field stars. On the same exposures, a naive centroid on the saturated core gives {naive}. Our wing fit gives {ours}. Gaia predicts {gaia}.
v.trust.how: Same exposures, same seasons ({from}: {n1} exposures, {to}: {n2}), same image coordinates. Naive methods: the brightest unsaturated pixel, and the brightness-weighted centre (first moment) of an 11 × 11 pixel box with the saturated core filled in as flat white. A season is the median of its exposures; no field-star calibration. Naive results depend on such choices (a 7 × 7 box gives {v7}); this is one common choice. Script: pipeline/naive_centroid.py.
v.ctrl.p1: Our method should find no motion where there is none. We ran it on {n} field stars around Barnard's Star that barely move (Gaia: under {pm} mas a year), in the same exposures, between {from} and {to}. The test stars never calibrate themselves: each half of the stars is calibrated with the other half.

s.barnard.what: A small, cool red dwarf star, {ly} light-years away: one of the Sun's nearest neighbours.
s.barnard.why: No other star crosses our sky as fast: about {pm}″ a year. If a method cannot see Barnard's Star move, it cannot see anything move.
s.barnard.shows: Its centre is too bright for the detector (saturated), so we measure it from the edges. It moved {shift} ± {err} from {from} to {to}. Gaia predicts {ref}.
s.eps_indi_b.what: Two brown dwarfs that orbit each other and, together, the star Epsilon Indi A, {ly} light-years away.
s.eps_indi_b.why: Brown dwarfs are "failed stars": too small to shine like the Sun, they glow mostly in infrared light, which is what SPHEREx sees.
s.eps_indi_b.shows: It moved {shift} ± {err} in {dt} years (Gaia: {ref}). Its position is about half an arcsecond from Gaia's, possibly because SPHEREx sees the infrared light of the pair, which is centred differently.
s.wise0855.what: The coldest brown dwarf known, {ly} light-years away. It is colder than the freezing point of water (about 225–260 K).
s.wise0855.why: It is the kind of object a Planet X search looks for: cold, dark, and almost invisible except in infrared light. Gaia cannot see it at all.
s.wise0855.shows: Only at {bins} µm, and faint. It moved {shift} ± {err} in {dt} years. The prediction from Spitzer measurements is {ref}.
s.luhman16.what: The closest brown dwarfs to the Sun: a pair about 6.5 light-years away.
s.luhman16.why: They were found only in 2013, in infrared images from NASA's WISE. Even the Sun's near neighbours can hide.
s.luhman16.shows: Not one of the five challenge targets: we ran it with our local engine. It moved {shift} ± {err} in {dt} years. The catalogue predicts {ref}.
s.rw_aur.what: A very young star system, still surrounded by gas and dust, about {ly} light-years away.
s.rw_aur.why: RW Aurigae A is known for deep dimming events, thought to be caused by dust passing in front of the star.
s.rw_aur.shows: At {um} µm it fades to {r} ± {e} of its {from} brightness by {to}, while at 1 µm it is {r1} times as bright. Its centre is saturated, so these are estimates from the star's edges.
s.r_dra.what: A red giant star near the end of its life, about {ly} light-years away, that swells and shrinks.
s.r_dra.why: Stars like this (Mira variables) change their brightness a lot; R Draconis does it every ~245 days. A good test of measuring brightness.
s.r_dra.shows: At {um} µm it drops to {r} ± {e} of its {from} brightness by {to}, as expected for a Mira. Its centre is saturated, so these are estimates from the star's edges.
how.lead: SPHEREx is a NASA space telescope, launched on 11 March 2025. It photographs the whole sky in 102 colours of infrared light, which our eyes cannot see. Four ideas explain what you see in a blink.
how.a.p: A 20 cm telescope sends its light to a dichroic mirror that splits it at 2.42 µm: shorter wavelengths go to three detectors, longer ones to the other three. Both sets look at the same 3.5° × 11.3° patch of sky at once, about 7 by 22 full Moons.
how.a.alt: Diagram: light from the telescope hits a dichroic mirror; short wavelengths go up to detectors D1 to D3, long wavelengths down to D4 to D6.
how.b.h: A rainbow filter on every detector
how.b.p: Each detector sits behind a linear variable filter: its colour changes smoothly from one edge to the other. Where a star lands on the detector decides which wavelength is measured. 17 channels per detector × 6 detectors = 102 colours, from 0.75 to 5.0 µm.
how.b.alt: Diagram: one detector covered by a filter whose colour changes in 17 steps from one edge to the other.
how.c.p: Between exposures the telescope steps a little across the sky. The same star lands on a different part of the filter, so each picture shows it in a different colour. That is why a star looks different from one SPHEREx picture to the next, and why our blink compares only pictures of the same colour (±6 %) from the same detector.
how.c.alt: Diagram: in three exposures the filter shifts under a star that stays in place, so the star is seen in three different colours.
how.d.p: One pixel covers {p}″, like a 2.5 cm coin seen from about {coin} m. Barnard's Star moves {s} a year: only {k} pixels. We can still measure it to a few hundredths of an arcsecond, because SPHEREx photographs the whole sky every six months (four times in its two-year mission) and every picture adds a measurement: {n} images in {ns} seasons for Barnard's Star, about {per} per season.
how.d.alt: Diagram: a grid of SPHEREx pixels; Barnard's Star moves {s}, about {p} pixels, in a year.
name.p: Fazari is named after al-Fazārī, a family of astronomers in 8th-century Baghdad who are traditionally credited with making the first astrolabes in the Islamic world (sources disagree whether it was the father, Ibrāhīm, or his son, Muḥammad). Muḥammad al-Fazārī also helped translate an Indian astronomical text, the Sindhind, into Arabic at the court of Caliph al-Manṣūr.

sk.m.method: Centroid: Gaussian fit to the unsaturated wings in native 6.15″ pixels, per exposure, converted with each exposure's SIP WCS; season = mean after clipping. {fits} of {exp} downloaded exposures fitted (bins loaded so far: {bins} µm). Relative astrometry (as pipeline/ASTROMETRY.md): isolated Gaia DR3 stars (10 ≤ G ≤ 17.5, RUWE ≤ 1.4, moved to each exposure's date with proper motion and parallax) are centroided the same way; their offsets, pooled per season and detector (shift, or shift + rotation + scale with ≥ 12 stars around the target, 3σ clipped), correct the target. A saturated target's wing-only centroid has a bias fixed to the detector (it flips when SPHEREx turns 180° between August and March); it is measured on saturated Tycho-2 stars in the same rows and removed.

ex.ab.1: SPHEREx images: NASA/JPL-Caltech, SPHEREx team, served by the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). The SPHEREx all-sky map layer is the IRSA SPHEREx DR1 HiPS (Caltech/IPAC).
ex.ab.2: Sky viewer: Aladin Lite v3 by CDS, Strasbourg Astronomical Data Centre (GPL-3.0; Boch & Fernique 2014, ASPC 485, 277), loaded unmodified from its published npm build.
ex.ab.3: Sky maps: DSS2 colour (Digitized Sky Survey, STScI/NASA; coloured and HEALPixed by CDS); 2MASS (University of Massachusetts & IPAC/Caltech, NASA/NSF); AllWISE (NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA, IPAC); for close-ups, Pan-STARRS DR1 colour (PS1 Science Consortium; images from STScI/MAST, HEALPixed by CDS). Maps are fetched from CDS, IRSA, ESA ESASky or STScI/MAST mirrors. Each map shows the sky in the years it was taken (DSS2 1975–1999, 2MASS 1997–2001, AllWISE 2010–2011, Pan-STARRS 2009–2015, SPHEREx 2025–2026), so fast-moving stars sit where they were then.
ex.ab.4: Names and positions: SIMBAD and Sesame (CDS, Strasbourg); Gaia DR3 (ESA/Gaia/DPAC) for the challenge targets.
ex.ab.5: Stars now and fast stars: Gaia DR3 from ESA, the European Space Agency (a Space Apps partner agency), processed by Gaia/DPAC (Gaia Collaboration, Vallenari et al. 2023, A&A 674, A1), via CDS VizieR (I/355/gaiadr3) and the ESA Gaia archive; positions moved to 2026.0 with Gaia proper motions. Near-infrared magnitudes of the fast stars: 2MASS and AllWISE through the Gaia DR3 cross-match.
ex.ab.6: Planet Nine band: Brown & Batygin 2021, AJ 162, 219; Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024 (arXiv:2401.17977). Planet Nine is a hypothesis; it has not been detected.
ex.ab.7: Cloud copies: SPHEREx images for the blinks are read from IRSA's public bucket nasa-irsa-spherex on the Registry of Open Data on AWS. Some DSS2 and Pan-STARRS map tiles come from STScI/MAST's public bucket on AWS (stpubdata), one of several mirrors.

pl.x.photMethod: Target flux divided by the mean of 2-5 comparison stars (each normalised to its median), per exposure; season value = median. Unsaturated target: forced EPSF flux. Saturated core: mean surface brightness in an annulus just outside the largest saturated core of the bin (same annulus in every season) - a wing-based estimate, flagged. Error = robust scatter/sqrt(N) of both seasons + the apparent season-to-season change of the comparison stars (comparison_scatter_frac).

pl.x.epsFinding: SPHEREx's infrared position is offset from the Gaia DR3 prediction by about +0.27″ E, −0.53″ N, the same in both spacecraft orientations, and larger at 4–5 µm than at 1–3 µm. This is consistent with the unresolved Ba+Bb binary (Gaia DR3 RUWE 4.30): the infrared photocentre differs from Gaia's G-band photocentre, plus orbital motion since 2016. Scattered light from Eps Indi A (6.7′ W) does not explain it: subtracting the local background plane changes the offset by < 0.02″, and Gaia field stars at the same distance from A show < 0.04″.

cm.h1: Comets moving through real SPHEREx images
cm.lead: These are known comets. JPL Horizons tells us where each one was at the moment each SPHEREx image was taken; we found the images that caught it, cut small boxes out of them and measured the comet ourselves: where it really is, how fast it moves, how big its glowing head (coma) is, and its brightness at each image's own wavelength. Nothing here is a discovery.
cm.specH: Brightness at each image's own wavelength
cm.selText: We started from all 4088 comets in the JPL Small-Body Database, computed where each one was at the mid time of every one of the 1.3 million public SPHEREx images (DR1 + QR3), and kept the images that really contain it (JPL Horizons positions). Then we read small boxes of the brightest predicted cases and kept the comets that are clearly seen.
cm.credits: Comet positions: JPL Horizons and the JPL Small-Body Database (NASA/JPL Solar System Dynamics). SPHEREx data: NASA/JPL-Caltech, served by the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), DR1 (doi:10.26131/IRSA678) and QR3 (doi:10.26131/IRSA662), read from IRSA's public bucket on the Registry of Open Data on AWS. Fazari, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Not endorsed by NASA.
cm.ours: What is ours: the selection, the SPHEREx pixels we read, the tracking, the stacks and every measurement on this page. Method and limits: pipeline/COMETS.md.

cm.specNote: {n} clearly detected images from {a} to {b} (comet {r} AU from the Sun). Each blue point is one image: a 12.3″ circle around the comet with the stars of other dates subtracted, divided by sunlight (a 5778 K blackbody) and set to 1 at 1.0–1.6 µm. Error bars: noise of the image plus 5 %. Dashed: smooth dust model (reflected sunlight with a slope, plus warm dust above 3 µm). Each band below is tested against a straight line through the images just outside it; the reflected-light points scatter {chi}× more than their error bars, so every test is widened by that factor. A band is named only at 5σ or more, with at least 2 images in it and images on both sides of it.

px.answer: Only if it is at the near end of its predicted orbit and bright in near-infrared light: in {n} strips of sky on that orbit our search finds half of the test bodies down to V {m50}, which is the predicted planet out to about {dhi} AU (it is predicted between {q} and {Q} AU), and it found no such body.

px.jump.h: Why one spot of sky cannot show it
px.jump.sub: SPHEREx comes back to the same sky every half year, and by then it looks from the other side of the Earth's orbit. A body a few hundred AU away therefore appears to jump against the stars (parallax), far more than it moves along its own orbit. We measured the size of the jump from the real exposure times of our five strips.
px.jump.jump: Jump between two visits half a year apart
px.jump.orbit: Own motion along its orbit in one year
px.jump.note: Jump = {lo}–{hi} thousand arcsecond·AU divided by the distance, measured between the {n} pairs of neighbouring seasons of our strips (the largest possible value is {max} thousand: twice 206 265). One pixel is {px}″. Own motion: a circular orbit. One year later the telescope looks from the same side again: the jump cancels and only the slow orbital motion is left.
px.jump.means: So such a body is never under the same pixel in two visits: a blink of one spot of sky between two dates cannot show it. Its detections have to be linked across a wide strip along the direction of the jump, which is what our search does, in strips {l1}–{l2}° long. What stops the search is brightness, not motion: we find half of the test bodies down to V {m50}, while a planet of {r} Earth radii at 500 AU would be V {v40} if it reflects 40 % of the sunlight, as Neptune does in visible light (V {v75} if it reflects 75 %). Whatever such a search links is a candidate, never a discovery.
px.chart.h: How faint we can find it, against how bright it should be
px.chart.sub: Curves: the visual brightness a planet of 2.07 Earth radii would have at each distance, for three assumed reflectivities. Lines with dots: the faintest brightness at which our search still finds half, and nine in ten, of the test bodies we added to the real images. Above our lines we would have found it; below them we would not.

Dots: each tested distance; the horizontal lines: all distances together. The brightness curves assume a grey body that reflects 0.75–2.4 µm light as well as visible light (see the assumptions below). White marks on the axis: the predicted distance at each strip.

Nine in ten is not reached at any brightness: even bright test bodies are found only {pl} % of the time (V {pm}), because a body that crosses a brighter star in one of the three seasons is lost. Dots: each tested distance; the horizontal line: all distances together. The brightness curves assume a grey body that reflects 0.75–2.4 µm light as well as visible light (see the assumptions below). In the {ni} exposures that had not covered these places before, which is independent data, the signal is {f2} where a real body would give about {e2}; random places in the same images do as well {pct} % of the time. The search links it again (signal-to-noise {f1}; a real body: about {e1}), and the {ni} exposures that had not covered these places before, which is independent data, show it too ({f2}; a real body: about {e2}; random places do as well {pct} % of the time). The result does not decide: signal-to-noise {f1} in all exposures (a real body: about {e1}) and {f2} in the {ni} exposures that had not covered these places before (a real body: about {e2}; random places do as well {pct} % of the time).

The two checks that explain these candidates, one track and real motion, were then made rules of the search itself, for the real strips and for their shuffled copies alike. In the same step we removed one part of the orbit fit that the test bodies had shown to be biased. With these rules the {f} strips give {links} links and {c} candidates, listed here. This pass is not blind: the rules were changed after we had seen the first two candidates.
px.res.text: In the {f} strips the search linked {links} sets of three detections, one per season. {c} of them were rare enough in shuffled copies of the same strips (chance probability at most 0.05, {n} copies each) to be reported as candidates. None was confirmed by the rule fixed before the search, and {pass} passed the checks below.

px.res.note: Two candidates are more than the shuffled copies predict for five strips (about 0.25). Shuffling cannot imitate a fixed source that shows up in both seasons of the same telescope orientation, so it underestimates that kind of chance link; the checks above catch it.
px.cand.what: Three detections (signal-to-noise {snr}) that fit one body {d} ± {e} AU away, about magnitude {mag} (AB). Chance probability from the shuffled copies: {fap}.

px.cand.v2: Its place is the same one year apart (it moved {mu} ± {e}″ in a year; a body on a circular orbit at that distance moves {circ}″): a fixed source seen in both seasons of the same telescope orientation, not something in orbit. What that source is, we have not established.

px.upper: Upper limit: no body brighter than V {m90} (found in 90 % of the tests; V {m50} for 50 %) between {d1} and {d2} AU in {f} strips covering {area} square degrees. V is for a grey body with the colours of sunlight.

px.upper.first: With the first-pass rules, tested on {n} bodies from {d1} to {d2} AU, the 50 % limit is V {m50} (bright bodies: {pl} %).
px.inj.sub: We added artificial bodies to the real images of the same five strips, on exact orbits and with the real image sharpness, and searched again with the same code. A body counts as found only if the search links it in three seasons and reports it as a candidate.

px.hon.h: What is measured and what is assumed
px.hon.measured: Measured: the limits come from {n} test bodies added to the real images. The search used {strips} exposures ({mb} MB read from the public archive as byte ranges; no whole file was downloaded).
px.hon.fu: The second look at the one remaining link read {mb2} MB more ({n2} exposures): {tot} MB of the {cap} MB we allowed ourselves.
px.hon.radius: Assumed: a mass of {m} Earth masses and, from it, a radius of {r} Earth radii (both from Brown & Batygin 2021). A larger or smaller planet moves every curve.
px.hon.albedo: Assumed: it reflects between 20 % and 75 % of the sunlight. Nobody has seen this planet; 75 % is a model of a cold hydrogen and helium atmosphere (Fortney et al. 2016).
px.hon.methane: Assumed, and probably too kind to us: that it reflects the light SPHEREx sees (0.75–2.4 µm) as well as visible light. Uranus and Neptune are several times darker there, because methane absorbs it. If Planet X is like them, it is one to two magnitudes fainter for SPHEREx than this chart says, and out of our reach at every predicted distance.
px.hon.area: We searched {area} square degrees: {pct} % of the band where the planet is predicted. Finding nothing there says almost nothing about whether it exists. Searching the whole band this way needs about 2 TB of image data instead of 1 GB.
px.hon.depth: The ends of a strip are covered by fewer exposures than its middle, so the search is shallower there; the limits above are averages over the whole searched area. Reading every exposure that touches a strip (about twice the data) would bring the whole strip to the depth of its middle.
px.hon.seasons: There are only three seasons of data. Three positions leave one coordinate free to test a link, so chance links happen. A fourth season would make them hundreds of times rarer and let fainter bodies be confirmed.
px.hon.cand: A candidate here is never a discovery: it is a place to look again. Both candidates of this run were explained by the checks above.
px.hon.second: The second pass is not blind. Its two rules were written down as checks before they were tried on test bodies, but they became part of the search only after the first pass had shown its two candidates. The headline limit on this page is measured with the second-pass rules; the first-pass numbers are given beside it.
px.hon.git: The times on this page (prediction 20:48, freezes 21:53 and 23:05) come from our working notes, which are not in the repository. Git shows less: PLANETX.md and the search code were first committed on 15 November at 00:16, after the search. The md5 of the v3b search code matches the committed file; the v3 file was never committed.
px.hon.old: Before this run the search used small cutouts with {n} exposures per season: it reached AB {before} and could not hold the track of a body closer than about 700 AU. Reading thin strips of every exposure made 250–1000 AU searchable; the reach for a planet that reflects 75 % is now {d} AU.
px.src.bb21: Brown, M. E. & Batygin, K. 2021, The Orbit of Planet Nine, AJ 162, 219 (arXiv:2108.09868): orbit, mass, radius, sky band.
px.src.b19: Batygin, K., Adams, F. C., Brown, M. E. & Becker, J. C. 2019, The planet nine hypothesis, Physics Reports 805, 1: a wider range of distances (why we tested out to 1000 AU).
px.src.f16: Fortney, J. J. et al. 2016, The Hunt for Planet Nine: Atmosphere, Spectra, Evolution, and Detectability, ApJ Letters 824, L25: reflectivity of a cold giant-planet atmosphere.
px.src.wl13: Wu, Y. & Lithwick, Y. 2013, ApJ 772, 74: the mass–radius relation Brown & Batygin use for the radius.
px.src.w18: Willmer, C. N. A. 2018, The Absolute Magnitude of the Sun in Several Filters, ApJS 236, 47: the colours of sunlight, to turn V into what SPHEREx sees.

px.src.cats: Catalogue checks: Gaia DR3 (ESA, Gaia/DPAC), 2MASS, AllWISE and CatWISE2020, through VizieR (CDS, Strasbourg).
px.src.skybot: Known Solar System objects: IMCCE SkyBoT (Berthier et al. 2006).

A visit averages many images, so the real limit is lower.

ts.lim.faint: For a faint one (magnitude {m}) the limit is {v}″ per year.
ts.lim.field: Anything moving faster than about {v}″ per year would have shown in these images.

ts.d.say: Our number, measured from these images alone, next to what the star catalogue says about the same object.
ts.e.say: How bright this spot is in each infrared colour. Every exposure sees it in a different colour, so the exposures together draw the curve.
ts.sp.sum.one: Built from {n} exposures of one visit: each exposure sees this spot in a different infrared colour.
ts.sp.sum.other: Built from {n} exposures over {s} visits: each exposure sees this spot in a different infrared colour.
ts.f.say: Did this spot get brighter or fainter between the visits? Each measurement is divided by this spot's own average brightness at that colour, so a steady source stays near 1.
ts.f.vRough: No change that can be trusted between the visits at this colour.
ts.f.vSteady: No significant change between the visits at this colour.
ts.f.vHalf: Faded to about half between {a} and {b} ({r}).
ts.f.vTimes: Became about {x} times brighter between {a} and {b} ({r}).
ts.f.ruleRough: The star is too bright for the camera at this colour: these are rough estimates from its faint outer glow, so only a change by more than a factor of two would count.
ts.f.ruleScale: A change counts when it is more than three times its uncertainty. Without comparison stars the brightness scale of a visit is good to about {p} % (our check against 2MASS and WISE), so that means a change of about a third or more.
ts.f.rule: A change counts when it is larger than 10 % and more than three times its uncertainty; the comparison is against ordinary stars in the same images.
ts.f.none: Nothing to plot here: no source is bright enough at this spot in any infrared colour, so there is no brightness to follow from visit to visit.
